I read Atlas Shrugged and The Fountainhead when I was a kid, and very strongly disagreed with her scenario wherein self-interest was a virtue of the strong, and everyone else were mostly leeches. But as I grow older, I'm starting to see her ideas about productive and non-productive people as (perhaps exagerated) real concepts in many contexts in society.

Does anyone have any reading recommendations for learning more about Objectivism and Rand's general philosophy?

Her novels are better than her pure 'philosophical' works in my opinion. You've read her best stuff. But if you want to bother:

http://www.intellectualconservative.com/images/capitalismtheunknownideal.jpg

http://2.bp.blogspot.com/-vQdggEIRAJ4/TqfCccENdDI/AAAAAAAAAEI/c1N0chgTIJk/s1600/philosophy-who-needs-it-ayn-rand-paperback-cover-art.jpg

https://leewoof.files.wordpress.com/2013/03/ayn_rand_the_virtue_of_selfishness.jpg

The Fountainhead is her best and I found Roark to be an inspiring character.

I lean Libertarian-ish, so you'd think I'd like her. But I have a "Never go full Libertarian" policy. Why? Because there comes a point where ideology is no longer realistic and practical. Ayn Rand went "Full Libertarian".

As for her "Objectionist" point of view. I'm half a mind with that. It's not that I entirely disagree. I just don't think it's the best way of going about things. For instance, I don't think philosophy of Epistemology should be mixed with philosophy of Ethics. Separate them, sure. But they don't belong under the same school. This is why I prefer the school of Greek thought. You have Stoicism which deals with Epistemology. And you have Greek Virtue which deals with Ethics. Both work together, but they are distinct and allow for some flexibility. Where as, Ayn Rands values are rigid.

On some level, I can read her fiction and appreciate it on the basis that it is (poorly written) fiction. But, I think she (and far too many others) take herself too seriously. I mean, I can watch Star Trek and enjoy it on the basis that, despite the socialist overtones, and the fact that I don't think such a Utopia is possible, at least they are good stories and are thought provoking. But, Ayn Rand isn't as good a story teller as Gene Roddenberry. So, the point goes to Mr. Roddenberry.

I suppose, if I were to recommend a good "Libertarian" book. It would be almost anything by the author, Neal Stephenson. Particularly, "Snow Crash". Most of his stuff is "pro-Libertarian", but it's the most realistic, in my opinion, because his "Libertarian Utopia" is very distopic in nature.

It's kind of like when people point out "Afghanistan", "Somalia", and the "Walled City of Kowloon" as examples of Libertarian values in action. But, then the "Full Libertarians" complain "Those aren't Libertarian, they failed because <insert excuse here>", but they are happy to claim the USSR is socialist despite the fact that it failed despite its <insert excuse here>.

I'd also recommend "Stranger in a Strange Land", by Robert A. Heinlein. It's a bit less heavy handed in the ideology department but more thought provoking than Ayn Rand's drivel.
